title: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Removing the special features of cellular automata, such as a rigid array of cells and parallel updating, does not prevent complex behavior from simple rules, so the phenomenon of complexity is universal and independent of the details of particular systems.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So this suggests that in fact the phenomenon of complexity is quite universal—and quite independent of the details of particular systems.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “Some Conclusions” (from p. 105), p. 105. Scope: all kinds of simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many distinct formalisms can be simulated now, so concrete subclaims are testable. No finite collection can resolve the universal generalization, and common metrics can privilege some representations.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define a preregistered set of computational formalisms lacking arrays or parallel updates and a common complexity metric, then compare the prevalence of complex trajectories. Repeated complexity across that set supports independence from those features, but cannot establish universality over all simple programs.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Complexity lacks a single representation-invariant operational definition.

All kinds and universal are unbounded scopes.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public simulators already cover the main discrete classes Wolfram uses, and repeating his removals of rigid grids and parallel update is a finite computation. The claim's scope is universality and independence from details of particular systems, which no finite catalog can exhaust. A survey can support or strain the claim for the classes studied in the chapter, which is a real but partial test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across several standard classes (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines), classify small rules into repetitive, nested, and irregular, and compare the fraction that are irregular. Complexity appearing in every class supports universality; a natural class whose entire small-rule space stays simple would count against independence from system details.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
There is no agreed enumeration of 'all kinds of simple programs,' so a survey of standard classes is only a sample.

Behavior classes are partly a matter of classification thresholds, which can make different systems look more alike than they are.
